title: Paramagnetism
short_intro: Paramagnetic substances are weakly attracted by external magnetic fields and possess a small positive magnetic susceptibility. Their atomic magnetic moments possess permanent dipole moments that tend to align weakly with an applied magnetic field.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of magnetic materials, susceptibility and permeability relations, qualitative behavior of paramagnetic substances with temperature.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Curie's Law, Curie-Weiss Law, quantum theory of paramagnetism, Langevin function, and molecular field theory.

prerequisites: Magnetic induction, magnetic field intensity, and magnetization vector

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Paramagnetism
bullets: Paramagnetic materials consist of atoms, ions, or molecules having a net permanent magnetic dipole moment due to partially filled inner electron shells (such as d or f orbitals).
In the absence of an external magnetic field, thermal agitation randomizes the orientations of these atomic dipoles, resulting in a net macroscopic magnetization of zero.
When an external magnetic field is applied, it exerts a torque on the atomic dipoles, tending to align them along the field direction against thermal randomization.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Susceptibility and Permeability
bullets: Magnetic susceptibility (χ) for a paramagnetic substance is small and positive, typically ranging from 10<sup>-5</sup> to 10<sup>-2</sup>.
The relative permeability (μ<sub>r</sub>) is slightly greater than unity, given by the relation μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ.
Magnetic induction B inside a paramagnetic material is slightly larger than the applied vacuum magnetic field B<sub>0</sub>, expressed as B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M) = μH.

concept_notes.heading: Curie's Law of Paramagnetism
bullets: Pierre Curie experimentally discovered that the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature T.
The mathematical expression is χ = C / T, where C is the material-specific Curie constant.
This law holds well at moderate temperatures and weak magnetic fields where thermal energy (k<sub>B</sub>T) significantly exceeds the magnetic potential energy.

concept_notes.heading: Curie-Weiss Law
bullets: At temperatures close to absolute zero or in the presence of strong molecular interactions, Curie's law deviates.
The Curie-Weiss law modifies the temperature dependence as χ = C / (T - θ), where θ is the Curie-Weiss temperature.
For pure paramagnets, θ is close to zero, whereas for ferromagnetic materials transitioning to paramagnetic behavior above the Curie point, θ equals the Curie temperature.

derivations.title: Classical Langevin Theory of Paramagnetism
derivations.conditions: Applied magnetic field B, absolute temperature T, N magnetic dipoles per unit volume each of magnetic moment μ<sub>m</sub>.
steps: Consider a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field B at an angle θ. The potential energy is U = -μ<sub>m</sub>B cosθ.

According to Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics, the probability of a dipole pointing in the solid angle dΩ is proportional to exp(-U/k<sub>B</sub>T) dΩ = exp(μ<sub>m</sub>B cosθ / k<sub>B</sub>T) 2π sinθ dθ.
The magnetization M is given by M = N μ<sub>m</sub> <cosθ>, where the average value <cosθ> is evaluated using the partition function integration.
This yields Langevin's function L(x) = coth(x) - (1/x), where x = μ<sub>m</sub>B / k<sub>B</sub>T.
For weak fields and high temperatures (x << 1), the series expansion gives L(x) ≈ x/3, leading to M = N μ<sub>m</sub><sup>2</sup> B / (3 k<sub>B</sub>T).
derivations.result: Susceptibility χ = μ<sub>0</sub> N μ<sub>m</sub><sup>2</sup> / (3 k<sub>B</sub>T) = C / T

derivations.title: Relation between Relative Permeability and Susceptibility
derivations.conditions: Uniform magnetic field inside a linear isotropic paramagnetic medium.
steps: Start with the fundamental magnetic field vector relation: B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M).
Substitute the definition of magnetic susceptibility, M = χ H, into the equation.
Factor out the magnetic field intensity H: B = μ<sub>0</sub>H(1 + χ).
Compare this with the macroscopic definition B = μH, where μ is the absolute permeability.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Susceptibility vs. Temperature (Curie's Law Graph)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola plot of magnetic susceptibility (χ) on the y-axis versus absolute temperature (T) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that susceptibility drops sharply as temperature increases, verifying inverse proportionality.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding the temperature dependence of paramagnetic materials.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Inverse Susceptibility vs. Temperature (Curie-Weiss Plot)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of 1/χ versus T intersecting the positive temperature axis at θ for ferromagnets turned paramagnets, or passing through the origin for pure paramagnets.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line equals 1/C, and the temperature intercept yields the Curie-Weiss temperature θ.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT numericals to determine the Curie constant and Curie temperature from graphical data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Quincke's Tube Method (Experimental Setup)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A U-tube containing a paramagnetic liquid placed between the pole pieces of an electromagnet such that one liquid meniscus is in a strong magnetic field region and the other is outside.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The liquid level rises or falls due to magnetic force acting on the volume susceptibility of the fluid.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Descriptive questions on experimental measurement of magnetic susceptibility of liquids.

solved_numericals.question: A paramagnetic substance has a magnetic susceptibility of 3.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> at a temperature of 300 K. Calculate its susceptibility at a temperature of 450 K.
solution_steps: Identify Curie's Law relation: χ<sub>1</sub> T<sub>1</sub> = χ<sub>2</sub> T<sub>2</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: The magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic salt is 0.01 at 27°C. At what temperature will its susceptibility become 0.02 according to Curie's Law?
solution_steps: Convert initial temperature to Kelvin: T<sub>1</sub> = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
Apply Curie's Law: χ<sub>1</sub> T<sub>1</sub> = χ<sub>2</sub> T<sub>2</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: A paramagnetic material follows the Curie-Weiss law with a Curie constant of 1.2 K and a Curie-Weiss temperature of 50 K. Calculate its magnetic susceptibility at 150 K.
solution_steps: Write down the Curie-Weiss law formula: χ = C / (T - θ).
Substitute C = 1.2 K, T = 150 K, and θ = 50 K.
Evaluate the denominator: T - θ = 150 - 50 = 100 K.

assumptions_and_limitations: Curie's law assumes independent magnetic dipoles without mutual interaction, which fails at very low temperatures or high field strengths where quantum saturation or cooperative magnetic ordering occurs.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Paramagnetic materials retain permanent magnetization after the external magnetic field is switched off.
common_misconceptions.correct: Paramagnetic materials lose their magnetization completely when the external magnetic field is removed due to rapid thermal agitation.
common_misconceptions.why: Retaining permanent magnetization is a characteristic of ferromagnetism, not paramagnetism.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance is negative.
common_misconceptions.correct: Magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance is always small and positive.
common_misconceptions.why: Negative susceptibility is exclusively a characteristic of diamagnetic substances.

quick_revision: Paramagnetism is characterized by a small positive susceptibility (χ > 0) and inverse temperature dependence (χ ∝ 1/T).
